clue.text: Mallards owner, Elizabeth's plan talked of ..

indicators.note: talked of says the word for plan is to be heard spoken, not seen written

parts.note: a plan of a place is a map

explanation.surface: Someone is describing the scheme drawn up by the woman who owns a house called Mallards.
explanation.walkthrough: In E. F. Benson's Mapp and Lucia novels, Miss Elizabeth Mapp owns Mallards, the house in the town of Tilling. The dots carry the sentence on into 4-across.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Mapp is the Benson heroine who lives at Mallards until her rival takes it over.

clue.text: Sterile, like The Iliad say, without Troy

parts.note: as means like, in comparisons

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside means the epic word goes round the troy letter

parts.note: Homer's Iliad is an example of an epic poem, hence 'say'
T is the abbreviation for troy, the system of weights for precious metals

explanation.surface: Calls something barren, like Homer's Iliad with Troy left out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking', but here it means outside. 'Troy' suggests the city of the Iliad but is troy weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Something aseptic is free of germs and contamination, as surgical instruments must be.

clue.text: Gertrude Agnew as captured by Sargent's novel

definitions.text: Gertrude Agnew as captured by Sargent
definitions.meaning: John Singer Sargent's 1892 painting Lady Agnew of Lochnaw shows Gertrude, Lady Agnew, a painted likeness of a titled woman
Henry James's 1881 novel about Isabel Archer

explanation.surface: Describes Sargent's famous society painting of Gertrude Agnew.
explanation.walkthrough: Sargent and Henry James were friends, which makes the pairing apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry James's 1881 novel follows the American heiress Isabel Archer; Sargent's canvas is a likeness of a titled woman.

clue.text: … with a rival of hers somewhere in Spain

parts.note: with can mean and, joining one thing to another
Lucia is Elizabeth Mapp's great rival in the Benson novels, so 'hers' points back to 1-across

explanation.surface: Continuing from 1-across: Miss Mapp and her rival are off somewhere in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue opens with dots because it finishes the sentence begun in 1-across; 'hers' means Elizabeth Mapp's.
explanation.definitionFit: Andalucia is the southern region of Spain, home to Seville and Granada.

clue.text: "Lake" novel by a pack leader

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new, so the letters of the quoted word take a new form

explanation.surface: Points to a novel called 'Lake' written by a wolf pack's leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book title's label but is the anagram signal on LAKE, making KELA.
explanation.definitionFit: Akela is the wise wolf leading the pack in Kipling's Jungle Book, and the title of a Cub Scout leader.

clue.text: The "Genius" author Goethe's three proems, regularly sent up

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held: The "Genius" author Goethe's three proems, regularly sent up (7). DREISER is fixed by the definition and crossings, but the wordplay letters contain no I, so no reading of this text gives the answer; probably an OCR misread, no scan.
annotationWithheld.clue: The "Genius" author Goethe's three proems, regularly sent up

clue.text: Poison Pen writer's left boot worn by Deighton?

indicators.note: worn by means the boot goes inside the name, as a foot is inside a boot the other way round

parts.note: Len Deighton is the British spy novelist
a welly is a wellington boot, a British rubber boot

explanation.surface: Imagines a poison-pen letter writer's left boot being worn by the spy novelist Len Deighton.
explanation.walkthrough: Poison Pen is a 1937 play by Richard Llewellyn, author of How Green Was My Valley. A welly (Wellington) is the British name for a rubber boot.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Llewellyn wrote the stage play Poison Pen as well as his famous Welsh mining-valley novel.

clue.text: Insane compiler's cryptic alternative title for "Les Mains Sales"

indicators.note: cryptic means puzzling and obscure, so the two words before it are scrambled

explanation.surface: A mad crossword setter offers a puzzling new English title for Sartre's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored: INSANE COMPILERS supplies all fifteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sartre's play Les Mains Sales (Dirty Hands) was staged in English under the title Crime Passionnel.

clue.text: Long, gripping article by an ancient Greek

indicators.note: gripping means the yearning word holds the article inside it

parts.note: to long for something is to ache for it
a is the indefinite article
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lengthy piece of writing that holds the reader, written by a Greek of antiquity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long, gripping article' reads like a description of a magazine piece, but 'Long' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Achaeans are Homer's name for the Greeks besieging Troy.

clue.text: Poet of note, right between Eliot and Sitwell?

parts.note: George Eliot was the pen name of the novelist Mary Ann Evans
me (or mi) is the third note of the sol-fa scale
Edith Sitwell was the English poet and critic

explanation.surface: Asks which notable poet ranks somewhere between T. S. Eliot and Edith Sitwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'between' sets the note and the right letter in the middle. 'Eliot' suggests T. S. Eliot, but George Eliot, the novelist Mary Ann Evans, is meant; Meredith was a Victorian poet and novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: George Meredith was the Victorian writer of the sonnet sequence Modern Love, and a novelist too.

clue.text: Film idols hiding with a rebellion's leader

indicators.note: hiding means the idols' word keeps the other letters out of sight inside itself

parts.note: idols of the screen are its stars

indicators.note: a word's leader is its first letter, here the first letter of rebellion

explanation.surface: Suggests a film whose idols are hiding out with the man leading a rebellion.
explanation.walkthrough: W, A and R (from 'a rebellion's leader') go inside STARS. 'Film idols' looks like one phrase, but 'Film' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Star Wars is George Lucas's 1977 space-opera film, a story that is itself about a rebellion.

clue.text: Duke saying, "Tennis-balls, my liege" one leaving overheard

indicators.note: overheard means the phrase for someone leaving is taken as it would be heard spoken

parts.note: someone who goes out, leaving a place, could be called an exiter

explanation.surface: A duke reports the Dauphin's gift of tennis balls to his king, then someone is heard going out.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Henry V the Duke of Exeter answers the king's question about the Dauphin's insulting present with the line 'Tennis-balls, my liege'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duke of Exeter is Henry's uncle in Shakespeare's play and speaks that line in Act One.

clue.text: Lines next to a river in the Bible

parts.note: an actor's lines make up a script
the Ural is a river flowing from Russia through Kazakhstan to the Caspian Sea

explanation.surface: Points to biblical lines written beside a river, like the waters of Babylon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' and 'river' suggest a verse about a biblical river such as the Jordan, but the definition is only the last three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something scriptural belongs to or is found in holy writ, the sacred text of the Christian faith.

clue.text: Sinatra song which has the longest sentence

definitions.meaning: a life sentence is the longest prison term a court can hand down, so 'this one is life' identifies it

explanation.surface: Asks which Sinatra song contains the longest sentence of lyrics.
explanation.definitionFit: A life term is the heaviest prison sentence; Sinatra's 1966 hit carries the same three words as its title.

clue.text: Frozen princess in stories about Norway

indicators.note: about means the word for stories goes round the letter for Norway

parts.note: ana is a collection of anecdotes or stories about a person
N is the international vehicle registration code for Norway

explanation.surface: The princess of Disney's Frozen appears in stories about Norway.
explanation.walkthrough: Anna is the younger sister in Disney's Frozen, set in a Norway-like kingdom, which makes 'Norway' blend into the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Princess Anna of Arendelle is the heroine of the animated film, sister to Queen Elsa.

clue.text: Maiden aboard loves seafaring work

indicators.note: aboard means the maiden's letter is put on board, inside the word for loves

parts.note: love is zero, O, in tennis, so several loves are a string of Os
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A young woman on a ship loves working at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden over in cricket is one where no runs are scored, abbreviated M on the scorecard.
explanation.definitionFit: Omoo is Herman Melville's 1847 book about his adventures as a sailor in the South Seas.

clue.text: A Roman poet and shepherd in conversation

indicators.note: in conversation means the word for shepherd is taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: to shepherd people is to marshal them, guiding them into order

explanation.surface: Pairs a Roman poet with a shepherd from his pastoral verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shepherd' looks like a noun from pastoral poetry, but it is the verb meaning to guide a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Martial was the first-century Latin writer of witty epigrams, born in Spain.

clue.text: An older Christian creed in Africa than Asia now

indicators.note: in points to letters sitting inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Claims an old Christian creed is now found more in Africa than in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'AfricA THAN ASIA Now'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athanasian Creed is a fifth-century statement of Christian belief in the Trinity, named after Athanasius of Alexandria.

clue.text: Trojan prince in posh, beautiful girl's clutches

indicators.note: in, with clutches, says the posh letter is held within the girl's name
clutches means held tight, so the posh letter sits inside the possessive name

parts.note: Helen of Troy was the most beautiful woman in the world, so a beautiful girl's is Helen's
U means upper-class, as in Nancy Mitford's U and non-U

explanation.surface: A Trojan prince falls into the clutches of a posh and beautiful young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from 1950s British slang about posh usage. Helenus was a son of Priam, and Helen herself fits the Trojan picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Helenus was a son of King Priam of Troy, a prophet who later married Andromache.

clue.text: Silver is one male sporting a piece of legwear half-heartedly

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: half-heartedly means half of the heart, the middle pair of letters, is lost

parts.note: a puttee is a cloth strip wound round the lower leg, worn by soldiers

explanation.surface: Describes a man showing off a piece of silver jewellery on his leg, half-heartedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver' looks like the metal but is Long John Silver, the one-legged pirate in Treasure Island. Removing one of PUTTEE's middle TTs leaves PUTEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Long John Silver lost a leg, so the pirate is someone with a limb removed.

clue.text: Witty publicity for spirits

parts.note: dry humour is witty in an understated way
ads, advertisements, are publicity

explanation.surface: Suggests a clever advertising campaign for whisky or gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spirits' looks like drink, as in an advert for liquor, but it means nature spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryads are tree nymphs in Greek myth, minor spirits of woods and forests.

clue.text: Book featuring Richard Parker's irrational existence?

definitions.meaning: Richard Parker is the Bengal tiger sharing the lifeboat in Yann Martel's 2001 novel
pi is an irrational number, so its existence, read cryptically, is the life of that number

explanation.surface: Asks which book shows a man called Richard Parker leading an irrational life.
explanation.definitionFit: Yann Martel's Booker-winning novel tells of a boy adrift with a tiger called Richard Parker; pi is an irrational number.

clue.text: "Half sunk a shattered visage lies, whose " (Ozymandias)

definitions.text: "Half sunk a shattered visage lies, whose " (Ozymandias)

parts.words: "Half sunk a shattered visage lies, whose " (Ozymandias)
parts.note: a quotation with its last word missing, from Shelley's sonnet about a ruined statue in the desert; the gap is the next word of the poem

explanation.definitionFit: Shelley's line continues 'whose frown, / And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command', describing the statue's scowling face.

clue.text: Lines to Satan in diabolical Petrarchan verse

indicators.note: diabolical means fiendishly messed up, so the letters before it are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Lines addressed to the Devil appear within some fiendish Petrarchan poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: The four words before 'diabolical' are all rearranged together, 'in' included.
explanation.definitionFit: Petrarch made famous the fourteen-line poem with an octave and sestet, so the Petrarchan form is also called the Italian form.

clue.text: Amateur players' cast performing

indicators.note: cast here means thrown about, so the letters of the players' word are rearranged

parts.note: the word is taken as written, without the apostrophe
on, as in on stage, means performing

explanation.surface: Describes an amateur dramatic company's cast getting up to perform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' looks like the actors in a play, but it signals the anagram; 'Amateur' is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur is a non-professional, someone without specialist training, as a layperson is.

clue.text: Song guide for the audience

indicators.note: for the audience means the word is to be heard, as an audience hears it

parts.note: to guide someone is to lead them

explanation.surface: A song meant to guide listeners at a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: Lied (said 'leed') is the German word for song, used in English for art songs by Schubert or Schumann.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lied is a German art song, typically for solo voice and piano.
